catalog_quote: Fivaz states the following in the introduction to his Reference Grammar of Oshindonga: “Ndonga, like all the other southern Bantu languages is a tone language, which is to say that the pitches on an utterance play a significant part in contrasts between lexical forms as well as in grammatical signalling. It is impossible to conceive of a comprehensive reference grammar of this language in which tone is not treated. However, having said this, it should be observed that the interpretation of the clearly audible pitches of the language in terms of a system is a complex matter. This description is in this important respect, no less than in any other, exploratory in nature. But, the tonal system in particular calls for more careful investigation than was possible in the time available for this study.” (Fivaz 1986:xix)

new_statements.rule_in_words: The primary grammar (Fivaz 1986) is reported to say only that Ndonga is a tone language in which pitch distinguishes lexical forms; no opened source says where word stress falls in Ndonga, and nothing found says whether there is penultimate prominence or lengthening.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None. Halme adds that Fivaz marks tone 'and discusses it to some extent', giving 'a number of (sometimes contradictory)' [statements], and that 'a detailed account of Ndonga tone is still lacking'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical tone ('contrasts between lexical forms'); the bracketed gap in the quote is text between two verified fragments that the snippet API did not return, and the closing words come from the same Fivaz 1986:xix quotation as cited by Halme. Halme's own penultimate-accent remark concerns Brincker/Tönjes on Kwanyama, not Ndonga.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources concern Oshindonga, the standardized Ndonga written variety of Oshiwambo (ndon1254, ISO ndo); Glottolog dialects Kwaludhi (kwal1254) and Eunda-Kolonkadhi (eund1238) are not separately described. Halme 2004 is a grammar of the sister language Kwanyama (kuan1247) and only reports on Ndonga second-hand; Brincker 1891's 'Oshindonga' column is 19th-century Ndonga. Hamakali & Mbenzi 2016 treats Oshikwanyama, and the Uushona papers treat 'Oshiwambo' generically.
